Losing "this" when a method is passed as a callback

Output: Hi Asha, Hi nobody, Hi nobody, Hi Ravi, Hi Asha. this is decided by how the function is called, not where it was defined. user.greet() has a receiver; fn() and the map callback are plain calls, so this is undefined in strict mode (in sloppy mode it would be globalThis). bind fixes this permanently, so even call can't change it. Passing user.greet to setTimeout or addEventListener loses the receiver in the same way. Fixes: bind, a wrapper arrow () => user.greet(), or an arrow class field.
Class methods vs arrow class fields

Output: 1, TypeError, true false, false. Class bodies are always strict, so the detached method gets this === undefined and this.count throws. An arrow field is created per instance in the constructor and captures that instance's this, so it is safe to pass as a callback (event handlers), at the cost of one function per object instead of one shared method on the prototype.
The Promise executor runs synchronously, and a promise settles only once

Output: A B C E D 1. The function passed to new Promise runs immediately, so B and C print synchronously; calling resolve does not stop the function. Once settled, later resolve/reject calls are silently ignored, so the value stays 1. The then callback is a microtask, so it runs after the current script (E) finishes.
?? vs || and optional chaining

Output: 50, 0, Untitled, '' (empty string), light, undefined, undefined, undefined. || falls back on any falsy value (0, '', false, NaN, null, undefined), so it wrongly replaces a real 0 or empty string. ?? falls back only on null or undefined. Optional chaining short-circuits the whole rest of the chain, so user?.name.first doesn't throw. You can't mix ?? with || or && without parentheses (SyntaxError).
const and Object.freeze are shallow

Output: prod ['a', 'b'], TypeError, [1, 2, 3], and the commented line would throw TypeError: Assignment to constant variable. const only stops reassigning the variable; the object it points to can still change. Object.freeze stops changes to the object's own properties, but nested objects stay mutable unless you freeze them recursively (deep freeze). In sloppy mode the write to a frozen property fails silently instead of throwing.
Prototypes, instanceof and hasOwnProperty

Output: Rex makes a sound, true false, true, changed, own changed, true true, true 'object'. Methods live on the prototype and are found by walking the prototype chain at call time, so changing the prototype affects existing objects. An own property shadows the prototype one. instanceof checks whether Constructor.prototype is anywhere in the object's chain. Use Array.isArray to detect arrays; class is syntax on top of this same mechanism.
Generators: what does each next() return?

Output: start then { value: 1, done: false }; got 5 then { value: 10, done: false }; { value: 'done', done: true }; { value: undefined, done: true }; and finally start, got undefined, [1, NaN]. Calling a generator function runs nothing; each next(v) resumes until the next yield, and v becomes the value of the paused yield expression (the first next's argument is ignored). Spread and for...of ignore the return value and pass no arguments, so x is undefined.
Object key order, delete on arrays, and sparse arrays

Output: ['1', '2', 'b', 'a', '-1']; 3 undefined false; [10, empty, 30]; [empty × 3]; [0, 1, 2]; 11. Integer-like keys come first in ascending order, then string keys in insertion order ('-1' is not an array index, so it is a string key). delete leaves a hole and does not change length; use splice to remove elements. Array methods like map and forEach skip holes, which is why new Array(3).map(...) does nothing; use Array.from or fill first.
null vs undefined: where do they behave differently?

Expression | null | undefined
typeof x | "object" (a historic bug) | "undefined"
Number(x), x + 1 | 0, 1 | NaN, NaN
Triggers a default parameter | No | Yes
JSON.stringify({ a: x }) | '{"a":null}' | '{}' (key dropped)
x == null / x ?? 'd' | true / 'd' | true / 'd'
Rule of thumb: undefined means "never set", null means "set to nothing on purpose". x == null is the one accepted use of ==: it checks for both.
== vs === vs Object.is()

Comparison | == | === | Object.is
'1' and 1 | true (coerces) | false | false
null and undefined | true | false | false
NaN and NaN | false | false | true
+0 and -0 | true | true | false
[] and false | true ([] → '' → 0) | false | false
Two different {} | false | false | false
Interview tip: use === by default; use Number.isNaN(x) to test for NaN. Object.is is "same value" equality, the rule React uses to compare state; includes and Map keys use SameValueZero, which also treats NaN as equal but +0 and -0 as the same.
Function declaration vs function expression vs arrow function

| function f() {} | const f = function () {} | const f = () => {}
Call before the line | Works (fully hoisted) | ReferenceError (TDZ); with var: TypeError, f is undefined | Same as expression
this | Set by the call | Set by the call | Taken from the outer scope
arguments | Yes | Yes | No (uses the outer one)
new f() | Works | Works | TypeError: not a constructor
Good as an object method | Yes | Yes | No: this is not the object
Rule of thumb: arrows for callbacks (they keep the surrounding this), method syntax for object and class methods.
typeof vs instanceof vs Array.isArray: how do you check a type?

Value | typeof | instanceof Object | Array.isArray
[] | "object" | true | true
null | "object" | false | false
() => {} | "function" | true | false
'hi' (primitive) | "string" | false | false
Array from an iframe | "object" | false for this window's Array | true
Rule of thumb: typeof for primitives and functions, Array.isArray for arrays, instanceof for your own classes. Check x !== null before trusting typeof x === 'object'.
